CALIFORNIA ABC TEST FOR WORKER CLASSIFICATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's own statutory worker-classification test — commonly called the "ABC test" — codified at Labor Code §§ 2775-2776, which was enacted to codify the California Supreme Court's decision in Dynamex Operations West, Inc. v. Superior Court (2018) 4 Cal.5th 903. It is prepared in connection with a working relationship between Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc.

California's ABC test is a separate and different legal test from the federal common-law control test addressed elsewhere in this corpus's own Independent Contractor Agreement document. The two tests ask different questions and weigh different things, and they can produce different answers for the very same working relationship between the very same two parties — satisfying one does not by itself show that the other is satisfied. California's ABC test is generally understood to be stricter and more protective of employee status than the federal common-law test.

This information sheet does not itself determine that Jordan Lee is or is not an employee or an independent contractor of Acme, Inc. under California law, does not apply this test to any specific facts, does not investigate or make any finding about any specific working relationship, and does not file anything with any agency or court.

THE STATUTORY PRESUMPTION OF EMPLOYEE STATUS AND WHO BEARS THE BURDEN
California law starts from a presumption that runs against independent-contractor status. Under Labor Code § 2775(b)(1), a person providing labor or services for remuneration is considered an employee rather than an independent contractor unless the hiring entity demonstrates that all of the ABC test's conditions are satisfied. As the statute's own text frames it, the default is employee status, and the burden of proving otherwise falls on the hiring entity — Acme, Inc., in a relationship with Jordan Lee — not on the worker.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "a person providing labor or services for remuneration shall be considered an employee rather than an independent contractor unless the hiring entity demonstrates that all of the following conditions are satisfied"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2775(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2775.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the presumption it states and where the burden of proof falls — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific worker is or is not an employee of any specific hiring entity. This clause states the presumption and burden only; the three specific conditions the hiring entity must satisfy to rebut the presumption are stated in a separate clause of this document. This document does not address how a hiring entity or a court applies this presumption procedurally in an actual dispute (for example, in litigation or before an agency), because that was not researched for this document.

THE THREE ABC TEST FACTORS — ALL THREE ARE REQUIRED
To rebut the presumption of employee status, Labor Code § 2775(b)(1) requires the hiring entity to establish all three of the following conditions:

(A) The person is free from the control and direction of the hiring entity in connection with the performance of the work, both under the contract for the performance of the work and in fact.

(B) The person performs work that is outside the usual course of the hiring entity's business.

(C) The person is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, or business of the same nature as that involved in the work performed.

The statute's own structure requires all three conditions, not a majority of them and not simply the most significant one. If the hiring entity fails to establish even one of the three — A, B, or C — the person is an employee rather than an independent contractor for the purposes this test governs, regardless of how the other two conditions come out.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "The person is free from the control and direction of the hiring entity in connection with the performance of the work, both under the contract for the performance of the work and in fact."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2775(b)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2775.)
  "The person performs work that is outside the usual course of the hiring entity’s business."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2775(b)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2775.)
  "The person is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, or business of the same nature as that involved in the work performed."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2775(b)(1)(C) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2775.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the three conditions it codifies and their all-three structure — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not an application of these factors to any specific worker's or hiring entity's actual working relationship. All three citations below are to the same statutory subdivision, Labor Code § 2775(b)(1), factors (A), (B), and (C) — they are not independent of one another, and are disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not survey the substantial body of California case law interpreting what "free from control," "usual course of business," or "customarily engaged in an independently established" trade mean on specific facts; that research was not conducted for this document.

WHAT THIS TEST GOVERNS, AND THE FALLBACK TO THE OLDER BORELLO TEST
California's ABC test does not present itself as the universal answer to every legal question about a worker's status. By its own terms, Labor Code § 2775(b)(1) states that the test applies "for purposes of this code and the Unemployment Insurance Code, and for the purposes of wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission" — that is, for California Labor Code purposes, unemployment insurance purposes, and the wage orders issued by the Industrial Welfare Commission. It does not, by this text alone, purport to govern every other body of law that might ask whether someone is an employee.

The statute also states its own fallback. If a court of law rules that the three-part test cannot be applied to a particular context on grounds other than an express exception to employment status, the determination of employee or independent-contractor status in that context is instead governed by the older, multi-factor test from S. G. Borello & Sons, Inc. v. Department of Industrial Relations (1989) 48 Cal.3d 341 — the decision the statute itself labels "Borello."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "For purposes of this code and the Unemployment Insurance Code, and for the purposes of wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission,"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2775(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2775.)
  "the determination of employee or independent contractor status in that context shall instead be governed by the California Supreme Court’s decision in S. G. Borello & Sons, Inc. v. Department of Industrial Relations (1989) 48 Cal.3d 341 (Borello)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2775(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2775.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the scope it states for itself and the fallback it provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not an exhaustive account of every California statute, wage order, or other context in which the ABC test or the Borello test actually applies. Both citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 2775, subdivisions (b)(1) and (b)(3) — they are not independent of one another, and are disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not independently verify the Borello multi-factor test's own content, having not fetched or quoted S. G. Borello & Sons, Inc. v. Department of Industrial Relations directly; it reports only what § 2775's own text says about when that decision governs instead. This document also does not survey case law on when a court has actually found the three-part test "cannot be applied," and does not address the statute's separate carve-out preserving express statutory or wage-order exceptions to "employee" status (§ 2775(b)(2)), which was not researched for this document.

THE BUSINESS-TO-BUSINESS EXEMPTION (LABOR CODE § 2776)
A separate statute, Labor Code § 2776, states that § 2775's ABC test and the Dynamex holding do not apply to a bona fide business-to-business contracting relationship, as the statute defines it, if the contracting business demonstrates that a list of specific conditions is satisfied. Where that showing is made, the older Borello multi-factor test governs the classification question instead of the ABC test.

The statute lists twelve such conditions. Among them: the business service provider must be free from the contracting business's control and direction over how the work is performed, both under the contract and in fact; and the contract with the business service provider must be in writing and must specify the payment amount, including any applicable rate of pay, and the due date of payment for the services. This information sheet does not restate all twelve conditions here; see the gap note below for which ones are omitted.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Section 2775 and the holding in Dynamex do not apply to a bona fide business-to-business contracting relationship, as defined below, under the following conditions:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2776 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2776.)
  "The business service provider is free from the control and direction of the contracting business entity in connection with the performance of the work, both under the contract for the performance of the work and in fact."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2776(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2776.)
  "The contract with the business service provider is in writing and specifies the payment amount, including any applicable rate of pay, for services to be performed, as well as the due date of payment for such services."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2776(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2776.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the business-to-business exemption it creates and two of its specific conditions — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific relationship between a hiring entity and a worker does or does not qualify for this exemption. All three citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 2776, its introductory clause and subdivisions (a)(1) and (a)(3) — they are not independent of one another, and are disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document quotes only 2 of the statute's 12 listed conditions in subdivision (a) — condition (1) (freedom from control) and condition (3) (written contract terms) — and does not restate conditions (2), (4), (5), (6), (7), (8), (9), (10), (11), or (12), which address matters including business licensing, a separate business location, the ability to contract with other businesses and advertise to the public, ownership of tools and equipment, rate-setting, control over hours and location of work, and a carve-out for work requiring a Contractors State License Board license; a reader relying on this exemption should review the statute's full text rather than this summary. This document also does not address subdivision (b) (governing an individual worker's status within a qualifying business-to-business relationship) or subdivision (c) (preserving rights under Labor Code § 2810.3) beyond noting their existence, and does not independently verify the Borello test's own content. This document does not determine that any specific relationship qualifies for this exemption and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — CALIFORNIA ABC TEST INFORMATION SHEET
I declare that I have reviewed the information above.

Executed on September 5, 2026 at Sacramento, California.
